2. Facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of this appellant, in short, are that 0.0913 acre of land appertaining to plot No. 4376 of CS Khatian No. 883 and 0.1087 acre of land appertaining to plot No of CS khatian No.881 (both the khatians now corresponding to RS khatian No. 757), containing 0.20 acre of land of mouja Radhaballav, police station and district Rangpur (as described in the schedule Ka of the pre-emption petition) belonged to one Hafez Mohammad Hossain Sowdagar who died leaving opposite party Nos. 2-10 as his heirs and heiresses. Subsequently, opposite party Nos. 5 and 6 transferred 0.0833 acre of land to the pre- emptor petitioner Shah Alam by a registered kabala dated 16-4-1992 whereby he became a co-sharer to the pre-emption petition Ka schedule land. Later, opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 transferred the case land, 0.0467 in area, as described in the schedule Kha of the pre-emption petition to the pre-emptee opposite party No.1 by a kabala dated 23-11-1994 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor petitioner and without service of notice upon him. Under the circumstances he sought pre-emption of the case land under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 11. The decision in the case of Sunil Krishna Banik and others vs Kailash Chandra Saha and others reported in BCR 1984 (AD) 243, which related to a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, reveals that in the trial Court the pre-emptees raised a plea of disability of the pre-emptor to pre-empt the case land on the ground of his having lost his co-sharership in the holding by separation of his jama through a mutation proceeding. In support of such separation the pre-emptees produced two rent receipts, two municipal tax receipts and another document (not specified) which were received by the trial Court as exhibits A, A (1), B, B (1) and C respectively but the learned Judge declined to consider them in his judgment because of their belated production and eventually allowed pre-emption. Being aggrieved the pre-emptees preferred an appeal before the High Court Division and during the pendency of the appeal filed an application under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure by annexing certified copies of application for separation of old jama which initiated two mutation proceedings, orders passed in the said mutation proceedings separating the old holding and two newly opened khatians as annexures A, A (1), B, B(1) and C, C(1) respectively and prayed for receiving the said documents as additional evidence regarding separation of the said jama. But the appellate High Court Division refused to receive them, as such, and dismissed the appeal. On appeal, their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed" the evidence offered by the appellants to prove that the respondent was no longer a co-sharer was already produced before the trial Court, but this was done only at a late stage of the trial. The evidence was not considered by the trial Court for this reason. It was not produced for the first time before the appellate Court. On the other hand, the exhibits referred to in their application for additional evidence could, if considered according to the appellants, have shown that the respondents had ceased to be co-sharers, particularly when the necessary issue to determine this point was already framed by the trial Court. "With the aforesaid observation their Lordships allowed the appeal and sent the case on remand to the High Court Division for disposal in accordance with law. The aforesaid observation by their Lordships left a clear indication that a co-sharer loses his co-sharership in the tenancy or holding by separating his jama through a mutation proceeding and cannot apply for pre-emption. 

 14. Now let us consider if, on the basis of the materials and evidence on record, learned court below correctly held that the petitioner-appellant separated his jama in respect of the land which he purchased from the opposite party Nos. 5 and 6 in the year 1992 and lost his right of pre-emption of the case land. Exhibit Gha, Mutation Register, clearly shows that mutation was approved in his name in respect of 0.0833 acre of land appertaining to the pre-emption petition schedule Ka land under the signature of Assistant Commissioner (Land) on 28-6-1993 vide Mutation Case No. 1354/92-93 DCR book of the year 1992/1993 (Exhibit Cha) shows that mutation fees and other fees amounting to Taka 28.50 were realised from him in connection with mutation case No.1354/92/-93 wherein a separate Khatian being No. 8399 with a jama of Taka 55.76 was opened anew in his name on 13-6-1993. Exhibit Chha, Rent Receipt Book, shows that land development tax ranging from 1396 BS to 1401 BS amounting to Taka 1163.50 paisa was realised from him on 23-1-1995 in respect of the said mutated Khatian being No.8399. Rent Collection Registers (Exhibit Uma, Uma (1) also carried particulars of such collection. By placing reliance on the said documents the learned Judge found that the petitioner-appellant, indeed, got his name mutated in 1993 in respect of the land which he purchased out of the case jote in the year of 1992 and already ceased to be a co-sharer in the case land when it was sold to the pre-emptee respondent No.1 in 1994. The aforesaid entries found place in those registers and receipt books in the usual course of business carried out by the public functionaries in the regular discharge of their duties. They have, therefore, presumptive value unless rebutted. The petitioner- appellant could not furnish any cogent evidence rebutting the same. Learned Judge rightly found that the petitioner-appellant had the opportunity to challenge the mutation proceeding to be a collusive and fictitious one by citing any of the co-sharers as a witness to prove that no notice was issued upon any of them in respect of mutation case No.1354/92-93 wherein his name was shown to have been mutated in respect of the land he purchased out of the case jote in 1992. But he refrained, which was quite meaningful. The learned Judge who closely scrutinised those registers and receipt books expressed with a profound belief that he found them to be genuine documents. There was thus overwhelming evidence on record showing a mutation case being No 13454/1992-1993 to have been legally started and completed at his instance opening a new Khatian bearing No. 8399 with a jama Taka 55.76 in his name on 13-6-1993 in respect of the land he purchased in 1992. It was not, therefore, much worthy of consideration if the mutation proceeding case record did not come before the court below on account of the circumstances, mention of which we have made earlier. The learned Judge thus rightly held that the petitioner having ceased to be a co-sharer in the case land he had no locus standi to claim pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.
